questions.prompt:
How should the API respond to this practical HTTP request?
POST /upload  multipart file=<small text file>
options: 200 JSON `{size: N, content_type: ...}`; the demo does not persist the file.
Keep all state in a global variable and skip authentication.
Ignore HTTP status codes and present failures as successful responses.
Return the same response to every request without checking its data.
questions.answer: 200 JSON `{size: N, content_type: ...}`; the demo does not persist the file.
questions.explanation: This is the expected behavior for `POST /upload  multipart file=<small text file>`. 200 JSON `{size: N, content_type: ...}`; the demo does not persist the file.

questions.prompt: Which design principle is correct for this topic?
options: Keep all state in a global variable and skip authentication.
Return the same response to every request without checking its data.
Uploads use multipart; filename and MIME are client claims, while size and content must be checked server-side.
Ignore HTTP status codes and present failures as successful responses.
questions.answer: Uploads use multipart; filename and MIME are client claims, while size and content must be checked server-side.
questions.explanation: Uploads use multipart; filename and MIME are client claims, while size and content must be checked server-side. `UploadFile` can spool large files, but a parser or proxy may receive the body first; endpoint checks alone are not enough.

questions.prompt: What changes if the important part shown in the lesson is omitted?
options: Return the same response to every request without checking its data.
Without size limits, a large body can consume resources; without content inspection, a misleading file type may be accepted.
Keep all state in a global variable and skip authentication.
Ignore HTTP status codes and present failures as successful responses.
questions.answer: Without size limits, a large body can consume resources; without content inspection, a misleading file type may be accepted.
questions.explanation: Without size limits, a large body can consume resources; without content inspection, a misleading file type may be accepted. An upload endpoint accepts `UploadFile` through multipart; the client controls the filename and MIME type, so do not trust them. This example reads at most 1 MiB and does not write to disk. Install `fastapi uvicorn httpx python-multipart`.

questions.prompt: Which action best prevents the common mistake from this lesson?
options: Ignore HTTP status codes and present failures as successful responses.
Return the same response to every request without checking its data.
Set compatible upload-size limits at the proxy, API, and application layers.
Keep all state in a global variable and skip authentication.
questions.answer: Set compatible upload-size limits at the proxy, API, and application layers.
questions.explanation: Set compatible upload-size limits at the proxy, API, and application layers. Never use a client filename as a server path; separately handle malicious content, oversize files, and archive bombs.
